author: researcher-mathematical
title: Per-sample bounded Gauss-Newton/LM MLE in log-conductivity attains near-CRB accuracy
text: The forward map F: k -> sensor time series is smooth and locally injective on [0.5,2]^4. Its Fisher condition number is moderate (median 62). The noise is small (sigma=1e-3). So the least-squares misfit is close to quadratic around the truth over most of the box. A bounded LM solve in log k with 3 starts will converge to the global minimiser for at least 95% of samples, and val rel_l2 will fall below 0.035 (within about 2x the CRB floor of 0.0185). It will clear the 0.05 success threshold. The forward model is known exactly: an explicit FD solve on 40 points and 200 steps, which is cheap. With i.i.d. Gaussian noise, MLE is asymptotically efficient. The harness CRB says the parameters are identifiable, with per-parameter relative std 0.5-2%. The log transform enforces positivity and tends to even out sensitivity across the k range, because diffusive time scales go as 1/k. Learned regressors trained on 3000 samples must interpolate a 4-D map from a 4x(time) feature space, and they usually plateau above the CRB. Direct inversion has no such approximation error, only noise-induced error plus failures to converge. context.forward reproduces the data-generating simulator exactly (no model mismatch) The misfit has no spurious local minima within the box reachable from 3 starts The noise is additive i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3, so unweighted least squares is the MLE LM is cheap enough per sample (~30 iters x Jacobian) that it fits within 120s per experiment over the val/test sets

assumptions: context.forward reproduces the data-generating simulator exactly (no model mismatch)
The misfit has no spurious local minima within the box reachable from 3 starts
The noise is additive i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3, so unweighted least squares is the MLE
LM is cheap enough per sample (~30 iters x Jacobian) that it fits within 120s per experiment over the val/test sets
data.falsifiable_test: Run on the val split and compare val rel_l2 to 0.035. Inspect the per-sample final residual norm: a converged sample should have residual^2 / (n_obs*sigma^2) close to 1. Falsified if val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if more than 5% of samples have residual chi^2 more than 2x the expected value (which would indicate local minima or non-convergence).
data.if_fails: If chi^2 is near 1 but rel_l2 is high, the CRB is optimistic and the error is irreducible noise sensitivity in k1/k4, so MMSE shrinkage is needed (Proposal 2). If chi^2 is large, there is non-convexity or LM failure, so we need better initialisation (learned init) rather than more iterations. A large timing overrun means amortised or hybrid approaches are required.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Learned initializer + LM refinement with posterior-mean (MMSE) estimator beats pure MLE on rel_l2
text: Because rel_l2 is a squared-error metric, the Bayes-optimal estimator under the uniform box prior is the posterior mean, not the MLE/mode. For the weakly determined boundary segments k1 and k4, and for samples whose truth lies near the bounds 0.5 or 2.0, the truncated posterior is asymmetric. Its mean then has lower MSE than the clipped mode. Combining three pieces should give val rel_l2 at least 10% lower than the best pure-physics (mode) run: a kernel ridge initializer on sqrt-features, which puts each solve in the correct basin; 15 LM iterations in log k; and a Laplace-importance-sampled posterior mean with 128 samples. This separates two error sources. (a) Basin and convergence failures: the learned init fixes these, and amortisation also means fewer iterations are needed. (b) Estimator choice under a bounded prior: the MMSE estimator fixes this. The CRB floor of 0.0185 applies to unbiased estimators. A Bayesian estimator that uses the box prior can go below it for parameters whose likelihood width (~2% of k) is not negligible against their distance to the bounds. That is relevant for roughly 5% of samples per edge for k1/k4. Kernel ridge suits the init because the inverse map is smooth and 3000 training points in a 4-D parameter space are dense enough for an RBF interpolant to reach a few-percent error. The Laplace approximation is adequate as an importance-sampling proposal (the posterior is near-Gaussian in log k away from the bounds) The kernel ridge init reaches rel_l2 around 0.05-0.10, which is inside the LM basin of attraction The gain from MMSE is measurable at the val sample size (750), i.e. larger than the run-to-run noise in rel_l2 of about 0.001 The training data are simulated from the same forward model (allowed)

assumptions: The Laplace approximation is adequate as an importance-sampling proposal (the posterior is near-Gaussian in log k away from the bounds)
The kernel ridge init reaches rel_l2 around 0.05-0.10, which is inside the LM basin of attraction
The gain from MMSE is measurable at the val sample size (750), i.e. larger than the run-to-run noise in rel_l2 of about 0.001

data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 against the best physics (mode) run from Proposal 1. Also report per-parameter relative error for k1 and k4 separately. Falsified if the hybrid posterior-mean val rel_l2 is not at least 10% lower than the best physics mode result, or if the improvement does not concentrate in k1/k4 (which would mean the gain came from initialisation rather than from the estimator).
data.if_fails: If the hybrid matches physics-mode but does not beat it, the posterior is near-Gaussian and untruncated for most samples, so the remaining error is the noise floor; final selection should then go to the cheaper method. If it is worse, the Laplace importance-sampling proposal is poor (heavy weight degeneracy), and a mode estimator should be kept.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + few-step LM refinement (log-space) reaches the CRB-limited regime
text: A torch_mlp trained on log-conductivity from standardized raw sensor traces (with noise augmentation at sigma=0.001) gives an initial estimate with rel_l2 ~0.05-0.10; 10-15 bounded LM iterations in log-space through the forward model then converge to the local MLE basin, giving val rel_l2 <= 0.035 (within ~2x of the CRB floor 0.0185), beating every pure library method. The forward model is cheap (40-point grid, 200 explicit steps), p=4, the noise level is known, and the Fisher condition number is moderate (~62). The MLE should therefore be near-efficient. The main risks for pure LM are local minima and wasted iterations from a prior-centre start. A learned initializer removes most of both. Log-space keeps positivity and evens out the relative errors across [0.5,2]. The likelihood is unimodal or near-unimodal within the MLP's error radius The forward call budget allows about 15 Jacobian evaluations per val/test sample within 120s The harness forward model is the same as the data-generating simulator (no model mismatch) Local Gauss-Newton curvature matches the 32-draw Fisher diagnostics

assumptions: The likelihood is unimodal or near-unimodal within the MLP's error radius
The forward call budget allows about 15 Jacobian evaluations per val/test sample within 120s
The harness forward model is the same as the data-generating simulator (no model mismatch)
Local Gauss-Newton curvature matches the 32-draw Fisher diagnostics
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against its own initializer alone and against pure physics LM from the prior centre. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid val rel_l2 > 0.035, or if it does not improve on the initializer by at least 30%.
data.if_fails: If refinement fails to improve on the initializer, the likelihood is multimodal or the forward model is mismatched, which can be checked from Gauss-Newton residual chi^2 vs the expected n_obs*sigma^2. If the initializer alone is already ~0.02, the learned map is near-efficient and refinement is unnecessary.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Hybrid learned-initializer + LM refinement reaches the Cramér–Rao regime (MMSE estimator)
text: The inverse map is locally well-posed: Fisher condition number is about 62 and the CRB rel_l2 floor is about 0.0185. With a cheap learned initializer, a few Levenberg–Marquardt iterations in log-k space through the exact forward model should converge to the basin of the true parameters. The posterior-mean estimator should then reach test-proxy (val) rel_l2 within a factor of about 1.5 of the CRB floor, i.e. below 0.03, and comfortably meet the 0.05 target. The forward simulator matches the data-generating process exactly: same explicit FD scheme, 40 nodes, 200 steps, known Gaussian initial condition and Dirichlet ends. Model misspecification error is therefore essentially zero, and the only irreducible error is sensor noise with sigma=1e-3. Per-parameter CRB relative std ranges from about 0.005 for k2 and k3 to about 0.02 for k1 and k4, so this is a mildly nonlinear, low-dimensional problem where Gauss–Newton is near-efficient. A learned initializer avoids wrong local minima. The posterior mean under the box prior shrinks the poorly determined k1 and k4 toward plausible values and reduces squared error versus the MLE near the bounds. Training and validation data were simulated with the same forward operator exposed by context.forward. Simulation fidelity is identical, so there is no discretization mismatch. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3 as stated, so the unweighted LM least-squares objective is the correct likelihood. The least-squares landscape in log k is unimodal within the basin reached by the ridge/kernel initializer for most samples. LM on 750 val plus 750 test samples with about 10–15 iterations fits in the 120 s per-experiment limit, given the cheap 40x200 forward model.

assumptions: Training and validation data were simulated with the same forward operator exposed by context.forward. Simulation fidelity is identical, so there is no discretization mismatch.
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma=1e-3 as stated, so the unweighted LM least-squares objective is the correct likelihood.

data.falsifiable_test: Compute val rel_l2 and compare it with the CRB floor of 0.0185. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.03. It is also falsified if the per-parameter error ranking does not match the CRB ranking (k1 and k4 worst). That would indicate either optimisation failure (local minima or too few iterations) or a forward-model/data mismatch. If the residuals are large, either the initializer leaves samples in wrong basins (raise extra_starts) or the simulator used for the data differs from context.forward, which is a simulation-fidelity issue to report.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Control: a purely data-driven noise-augmented MLP is limited by approximation and sample error, not by noise
text: This is a competing explanation test for where the error comes from. A torch MLP trained on 3000 simulated samples with noise augmentation will reach val rel_l2 between 0.03 and 0.06. That is clearly worse, by at least 30% relative, than the forward-model-refined hybrid. If so, the data-driven error is dominated by function-approximation and finite-sample error, not by measurement noise. If instead the MLP matches the hybrid within 10%, both are noise-limited and the forward model adds no value at this noise level. This gives an evaluation-design control. With only 3000 training draws in a 4-D parameter space, typical point spacing in k is about 1.5/3000^(1/4), or roughly 0.2 per axis. Interpolation errors of a few percent are plausible for k1 and k4, which affect the signals only weakly. Comparing the MLP against the hybrid separates noise-limited error from model-limited error. Noise augmentation at the true sigma is used so the network does not overfit to one noise realization per sample, which matches the measurement model. Feature noise in the training data has the same sigma=1e-3 as validation and test, so augmentation at noise_scale matching the standardized sigma is faithful. The train, val and test parameter distributions are all the stated uniform prior, so there is no covariate shift. Log-transforming the targets gives a near-symmetric target distribution on [log 0.5, log 2] and helps relative error.

The train, val and test parameter distributions are all the stated uniform prior, so there is no covariate shift.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Physics-informed feature reformulation: amortized regression on log-temperatures with noise augmentation reaches near-CRB accuracy without per-sample solves
text: The inverse map from sensor data to k is smooth but highly nonlinear in raw temperatures. Diffusion makes the signal decay roughly exponentially with rate proportional to k, so log temperature makes the map closer to linear in log k. A torch MLP on log features, with a log target and noise augmentation, will get val rel_l2 < 0.04. That is a purely amortized estimator within ~2x of the CRB floor and with no forward solves at inference. This challenges the assumption that iterative physics solves are needed for near-optimal accuracy. Under a heat-kernel picture, log u(x_s, t) ≈ -(x_s-0.5)^2/(4 k_eff t) + const, which is affine in 1/k_eff. Log features should therefore linearize the inverse problem, and 3000 samples in 4-D parameter space is a dense covering (~7 per axis on a 4-D grid). Noise augmentation enforces the correct noise model so the net learns the posterior-mean-like regression function. Temperatures at sensors stay positive above the noise level, so the log feature is well defined. The harness handles nonpositive values; otherwise early-time far sensors with u ≈ 0 add noise amplification. 3000 training samples suffice for an MLP to approximate the 4-D inverse map to ~3% accuracy The training noise distribution matches validation

assumptions: Temperatures at sensors stay positive above the noise level, so the log feature is well defined. The harness handles nonpositive values; otherwise early-time far sensors with u ≈ 0 add noise amplification.

title: Per-sample bounded LM MLE in log-conductivity is statistically efficient relative to the mean-aggregated per-sample CRB; paired control for MMSE arms
text:
The forward model matches the data and the misfit is near-quadratic at sigma = 1e-3. Under these conditions, the bounded log-LM MLE (3 starts, 30 iterations) is efficient.

Predictions on the full val split:
- rel_l2 / floor_mean <= 1.15, where floor_mean = sqrt(mean_i tr(CRB_i)/||k_i||^2) on the same val samples.
- rel_l2 < 0.025 in absolute terms.
- Residuals pass a chi^2_{n-4} calibration check.
- On interior samples (truth more than 2 GN std from every bound), per-parameter RMSE divided by per-sample CRB std lies in [0.8, 1.3]. The pilot gave 0.0190 on n = 60, which is 1.03x the median-CRB floor, with calibrated coverage.

The full split tests two things. First, whether efficiency holds across the tail of the val distribution, where shielded configurations inflate the per-sample CRB. Second, whether the floor itself is heavier-tailed than the median suggests.

The run also provides the paired control for the MMSE arms (P-010, P-012) and the hybrid arm (P-013). Forward model matches the simulator. Measured: oracle residual std 0.000995 vs 0.001. The per-sample CRB uses the same forward Jacobian as the GN covariance. rel_l2 aggregation is taken from the harness definition, and the floor uses the same aggregation. No spurious minima are reachable from 3 starts. Checked by start spread. n_obs per sample is taken from the harness (800 if all time steps are observed).

data.if_fails:
Each failure mode points to a different conclusion:
- (i) fails with chi^2 calibrated: the excess is bias or a local-minimum problem, so inspect the start spread.
- (ii) only fails: the tail is intrinsically hard, so the estimator is efficient but the floor is heavy-tailed, and Bayesian shrinkage (P-010) is the only lever.
- (iii) fails: there is a noise or model mismatch in a subset, so inspect it by configuration.
- (v) fails on interior samples: the FD Jacobian or the LM termination is inadequate.
data.response_to_critic:
I accept all three challenges. The method is unchanged; the test and the floor are tightened.

(1) chi^2 threshold. If every step is observed, n_obs = 4 sensors x 200 steps = 800 per sample. The facts only say 'discrete times, finite window', so I cannot verify that. The per-sample threshold is now the chi^2_{n-4} 0.975 quantile divided by (n-4), using whatever n the harness reports (about 1.10 at n = 800, about 1.20 at n = 200). The null rate is then 2.5%, and the test is falsified only if more than 5% of samples exceed it.

(2) Floor. The headline efficiency is now rel_l2 divided by the mean-aggregated per-sample floor, sqrt(mean_i tr(CRB_i)/||k_i||^2), computed on the same 750 val samples with the harness's rel_l2 aggregation. The median-based 0.0185 is no longer the anchor. I accept the shielding counterexample (k1 = 1.98, k2 = 0.55): an efficient estimator can still have a large error there, so the absolute 0.025 bar is kept only as a secondary check.

(3) Bounds. The per-parameter efficiency ratio is now evaluated only on the stratum where the truth is more than 2 GN std from every bound. Near-bound samples are reported separately and are not falsifying.

Hypothesis 2 is falsified if either of the following holds:

data.if_fails:
Three outcomes to distinguish:
- Mode arm still far worse than P-009: the custom_solver forward/feature alignment or the FD Jacobian is broken. Abandon the custom_solver route and test truncation post-hoc on harness physics fits.
- Mode arm matches but mean is no better than mode: box truncation is negligible at sigma = 1e-3. The clipped MLE is effectively Bayes-optimal for rel_l2, so select the cheapest efficient physics arm.
- Mean is worse: the linear extrapolation or the Laplace approximation is inaccurate near the bounds, so the exact posterior mean would need importance sampling with in-box forward calls (P-012).
data.response_to_critic:
The pilot is decisive negative evidence: rel_l2 0.0792 on n = 60, against 0.0190 for P-009 on the same pilot protocol. That is about 4x worse, so a 2-7% truncation effect cannot explain it. The solver itself failed.

The most likely cause is the one the critic flagged, compounded by my loose clamp [0.25*lo, 2*hi]. That clamp let the k-space GN iterate, and its FD perturbations, reach k up to 4. There the explicit scheme can be unstable or inaccurate, and the out-of-box Jacobian is unreliable. A k-space LM started from the prior centre is also worse-conditioned than the log-space LM that worked in P-009. I record the original design, which evaluated the forward outside the box, as a negative result.

Revised design:
(a) Bounded LM in log k with the forward evaluated only inside [0.5, 2]^4. This uses one-sided backward FD steps at the upper bound and 2 starts (prior centre and geometric centre).
(b) The unconstrained centre the truncated mean needs is obtained without any out-of-box forward call. It is a single linear GN extrapolation from the in-box mode: m = theta_box + (J^T J)^-1 J^T r. This is zero for interior optima and points outward along active bounds.

title: Is the amortization gap data-limited? Fresh simulated training data (4x) with a box-aware logit target, as the missing learning-curve control

The logit-box target z = logit((k-lo)/(hi-lo)) makes predictions respect the prior support by construction. That means the gap is approximation/regression-to-mean error concentrated on the weakly identified edge segments, not noise-limited. The physics MLE pilot already reaches about 1.03x the CRB, so the interesting question is no longer whether 0.05 is reachable. It is why amortized inference falls short of the floor and where. The r_j shape diagnostic and the 300→3000 scaling exponent separate three explanations: data limitation, approximation/shrinkage, and noise. text: The amortized log-MLP initializer (identical to P-015) lies within the near-quadratic basin of the per-sample MLE. So 5 bounded log-space LM iterations, with no extra starts, bring val rel_l2 below 0.025. The result is within 10% of P-009's 30-iteration multistart MLE on the same samples, and the residual k1/k4 gap closes in the same proportion as k2/k3. This tests whether the forward model corrects the learner's approximation error, as the critic suggested, and how cheaply.
